beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Shyam Sundar. When a lot is released, the question isn't only whether someone approved it. It's whether the evidence behind it holds up.

show.event: corrects 'approved' to 'backed by evidence' on the spoken correction

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive question and corrects it to the real one: is the release backed by evidence.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: My final project is called StopLine. It's a small Python tool that checks a proposed decision on a factory quality incident against the evidence that decision cites.

beats.narration_text: When it's finished, it will be a public repository with a command-line tool, a synthetic test set, tests, and an evaluation report that lists where it fails.

beats.narration_text: It gives one of three answers: human review required, needs more evidence, or accept for review. The most cautious one wins. It never approves anything. Accept only means a person may now look at it.

beats.narration_text: A first version exists today. Claude Code wrote most of the code with me on October fourteenth, and I've since reviewed every check myself. Here is the real output: seventeen synthetic incidents, one outcome each, and twelve tests passing. Every incident and number in it is made up for testing.
beats.new_visual_element: A terminal panel redraws three real lines from reports/cli_output

shot.visual_intent: A terminal panel redraws three real lines from reports/cli_output.txt and reports/test_run.txt (run 2026-10-14). Caption: real run, synthetic data.
shot.motion_claim: A terminal panel redraws three real lines from reports/cli_output.txt and reports/test_run.txt (run 2026-10-14). Caption: real run, synthetic data.

beats.narration_text: The real alternative is SAP's quality module, where a usage decision accepts or rejects a lot. From my experience in SAP, it already checks that results are recorded, that they belong to the right lot, and that they come before the decision, and it can refuse or warn. It checks structured results, not the written justification. So, honestly, StopLine doesn't beat SAP yet. The question I'll test is whether checking written claims catches something SAP's checks don't, and right now my own tool misses that case too.

beats.narration_text: It's aimed at supply chain manager roles. When a lot goes on hold, supply waits on the decision to release, rework, or scrap it. A hiring manager runs one command, sees an outcome for each incident, and opens the report, in under a minute.

beats.narration_text: It shows verification: every claim checked against a record. Evaluation: a labelled test set and a report. And escalation: what it can't check goes to a person. It does not show an agent loop or prompt contracts. There's no language model in it.

beats.narration_text: Out of scope, on purpose: real factory data, and any model making the decision. The first piece, the command-line run, already works, and the saved output shows it ran.

beats.narration_text: The risk is already visible. Two of seventeen cases get it wrong. One claim says all suspect units are contained, citing four hundred units from a lot of twelve hundred. The number is right, the sentence misleads, and every rule passes. A check is only as strict as the information it's given. I'll add harder cases and keep escalation as the default.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? I had an idea of how to bring it to life, so I took it on. It's a mix. What I already bring is supply chain work: supplier scorecards and root-cause reviews in SAP as an analyst, and a Six Sigma Green Belt. What's new is writing and testing a verification engine like this myself, with a labelled test set and an honest failure report, and blending supply chain with AI in a way I can check.

beats.narration_text: What exists today: the engine, the data, the tests, and an honest report. What will exist: harder test cases, fixes for the misses, and a real test against SAP's checks. That's StopLine.
